ch01.anchor: toward a solution on the battlefields of the class struggle
ch01.note: Isaacs writes as a Marxist, and specifically from the Trotskyist opposition to Stalin; the framing of Chinese history as a sequence of class struggles driving toward revolution is his lens throughout, and later notes flag where it shapes a factual claim.

Karl Marx’s term for societies in which a centralized state, controlling irrigation and public works, extracts surplus from largely self-sufficient villages, supposedly leaving them static for centuries. It was debated among Marxists in the 1920s–30s, later suppressed in the USSR, and is rejected by most historians today (a real term of Marx’s; its application to China is contested).

ch01.anchor: the attempted reforms of Wang Mang
ch01.note: Wang Mang (c. 45 BCE–23 CE) seized the throne from the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE, China’s formative empire) and ruled as the Xin dynasty (9–23 CE), decreeing a sweeping nationalization of land before he was overthrown. His usurpation fell between the Western and Eastern Han, not strictly “after the fall of the Han” as Isaacs has it (broadly corroborated; the dating is loose).

Wang Anshi (1021–1086), chief councillor of the Song, whose New Policies of 1069 included state farm loans and price stabilization. They came more than a century into the Song (Isaacs’s “Sung,” 960–1279), not at its rise after the T’ang (618–907) (a real reformer; the timing is compressed).

The Manchus, a people from beyond the Great Wall in the northeast, conquered China in 1644 and ruled as the Ch’ing (Qing) dynasty until 1912 — the last imperial dynasty. As non-Han rulers they imposed the queue and were the target of the anti-dynastic, ethnic-nationalist feeling Isaacs describes.
“Cathay” is an old European name for China, from the Khitan people; by the twentieth century it was archaic and literary.
“The Celestial Empire” was a nineteenth-century Western epithet for imperial China, echoing the emperor’s title as the Son of Heaven; Isaacs uses it with irony.

The two wars Britain (joined by France in the second) fought to force open the China trade and protect the opium traffic: the First Opium War (1839–42), ended by the Treaty of Nanking, and the Second, or “Arrow,” War (1856–60), whose Treaties of Tientsin were signed in 1858. Isaacs dates them by those treaties, not by the fighting (corroborated).
A durable yellowish cotton cloth woven in China and named for Nanking, once a staple export until British machine-made cottons destroyed the trade.

ch01.anchor: set up the system of extraterritoriality
ch01.note: The treaty privilege by which foreigners in China answered to their own countries’ laws and courts, not Chinese law, and were exempt from Chinese taxation — a central grievance of the nationalist movement, not abolished until 1943.

Regions where one power claimed priority for its railways, loans, and mines — Britain in the Yangtze valley, Japan in the northeast, France in the far south, Russia in Manchuria — stopping short of outright colonies.

ch01.anchor: arrived at Canton laden with silver
ch01.note: Canton (modern Guangzhou), the great southern port and, before 1842, the only city where Westerners could trade; later the base of the overseas-Chinese and revolutionary movements. (On the older spellings Isaacs uses throughout — Canton, Peking, Nanking — see the note on this edition; the modern pinyin forms are in the glossary.)

“Mandarin,” from Portuguese, was the Western name for a Chinese scholar-official of the imperial bureaucracy, ranked by examination degree and by the colored button on his cap (the “mandarin’s button” Isaacs mentions below).

The Cohong (gonghang) was the guild of licensed Chinese merchant houses at Canton that, before 1842, monopolized all trade with Westerners; its members grew immensely rich and buffered the government from the foreigners.

The tael (abbreviated Tls. in the trade tables later in the chapter) was a Chinese unit of silver by weight — the customs, or Haikwan, tael was about 37.8 grams — not a coin, used for large sums and government accounts; 200,000 taels denotes a very great fortune.

A comprador (from Portuguese, “buyer”) was the Chinese manager who ran a foreign firm’s dealings with the local market. Isaacs makes this class — brokers for foreign capital, often also landlords — central to his account of how imperialism fastened onto Chinese society (a real social category; the emphasis is his).

The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), a quasi-Christian mass uprising that grew from the “God-worshippers” of the far south, took Nanking in 1853 as its “Heavenly Capital,” and held much of the Yangtze valley until 1864. With some 20–30 million dead it was among the deadliest wars in history; Isaacs’s “eleven years” counts from the Nanking capital to the fall (corroborated).
Kwangsi (modern Guangxi), the far-southern province where Hung’s God-worshippers first rose.

Hong Xiuquan (1814–1864), the Taiping leader, who after a series of visions proclaimed himself the younger brother of Jesus and, at Nanking, “Heavenly King” (Tianwang); he died as the city fell in 1864. Isaacs’s spelling “Hung Tsui-chuen” is idiosyncratic even for the 1930s (standard Wade-Giles: Hung Hsiu-ch’üan).

The Ming (1368–1644) was the last Han-Chinese dynasty before the Manchu conquest; restoring Ming dress and letting the hair grow (rejecting the queue) proclaimed a Han restoration against the Manchus.

The queue — shaved forehead and long braid — was imposed on Chinese men by the Manchus after 1644 on pain of death; cutting it off was itself an act of rebellion, which is why the Taipings and the 1911 revolutionaries did so.

Charles George “Chinese” Gordon (1833–1885), the British officer who led the Western-officered “Ever-Victorious Army” against the Taipings and was later killed at Khartoum. Isaacs’s sardonic phrasing underscores that Christian powers crushed the Taipings’ own Christianity.

Zeng Guofan (1811–1872), the Hunan official whose provincial army broke the Taiping Rebellion; a pillar of the landed gentry and of the “self-strengthening” movement (the post-1860 drive to adopt Western arms and industry while preserving the old order) that followed.

Li Hongzhang (1823–1901), the most powerful Chinese official of the late Qing: Taiping-war commander, founder of arsenals, steamship and mining companies, and negotiator of the treaties ending the wars with Japan and the Boxers. Isaacs casts him as the “compradore-in-chief” who launched China’s first modern industries.

The Triads (Tiandihui, “Heaven and Earth Society”) were sworn brotherhoods, part secret society and part criminal fraternity, with a standing “oppose the Qing, restore the Ming” tradition. Their Small Sword Society held the walled Chinese city of Shanghai from 1853; the foreign guns Isaacs mentions intervened in 1854.
The Yuanmingyuan, the emperors’ vast garden-palace outside Peking, looted and burned by British and French troops in October 1860 to force China’s submission — a byword for imperialist vandalism.
Annam is an old Western name for central Vietnam; with Cambodia and Tonkin it became part of French Indochina in the 1880s.

The Meiji Restoration of 1868 overthrew Japan’s shogunate and launched rapid, state-led industrialization and military modernization; within a generation Japan defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905). Isaacs contrasts Japan’s success with China’s blocked development.
Manchuria is the northeastern region of China (the Manchu homeland), rich in land and minerals and coveted by both Russia and Japan; Japan would seize it in 1931.
The First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95), fought chiefly over Korea, ended in a crushing Chinese defeat that exposed the failure of Qing “self-strengthening” and set off the scramble for concessions.

The treaty of April 17, 1895 ending the Sino-Japanese War: China recognized Korea’s independence, ceded Taiwan and the Liaotung Peninsula (soon returned under Russian, French, and German pressure), paid a 200-million-tael indemnity, and — as Isaacs stresses — opened China to foreign-owned factories, a right extended to all the powers by most-favored-nation clauses (corroborated).

ch01.anchor: Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, Herbert Spencer, and Thomas Huxley
ch01.note: These British liberal and evolutionary thinkers reached Chinese reformers mainly through the celebrated translations of Yen Fu (Yan Fu) around 1900; the social-Darwinist ideas of Spencer and Huxley — struggle, adaptation, survival — especially marked the reform generation.

ch01.anchor: gained the ear of the young emperor Kwang Hsu
ch01.note: The Kuang-hsü, or Guangxu, Emperor (reigned 1875–1908) backed the 1898 reforms and was placed under palace arrest by the Empress Dowager for the rest of his life; he died in 1908, a day before her (forensic tests in 2008 confirmed arsenic poisoning).
The Hundred Days’ Reform (June–September 1898): a burst of modernizing edicts under Guangxu, ended by the Empress Dowager’s coup. Isaacs uses it to show the impotence of reform imposed from above.

ch01.anchor: resistance to the reforms crystallized around the Empress Dowager
ch01.note: Cixi (1835–1908), the Empress Dowager who dominated the Qing court for nearly half a century. She crushed the 1898 reforms, later backed the Boxers, and only then conceded halting constitutional change — Isaacs’s “last vigorous representative” of the dynasty.

Kang Youwei (1858–1927), the scholar who recast Confucius as a reformer and led the 1898 “Hundred Days,” and his brilliant disciple Liang Qichao (1873–1929), China’s most influential journalist-reformer. Both fled abroad after the coup and thereafter argued for constitutional monarchy, not revolution — which is why Isaacs later shows students turning away from Kang.

ch01.anchor: the I Ho Chuan (Fists for the Protection of Public Peace)
ch01.note: The Yihequan, “Boxers United in Righteousness,” a north-China martial-arts movement whose anti-foreign, anti-Christian rising the court turned outward in 1900; Isaacs’s gloss “Fists for the Protection of Public Peace” is a loose rendering of the name.

The settlement of September 7, 1901 imposed by the powers after the Boxer Rising: an indemnity of 450 million taels (about US $333 million, payable with interest over 39 years), foreign legation guards, and razed forts. Isaacs’s “U.S. $350,000,000” rounds the figure up slightly (substantially corroborated).

ch01.anchor: a war fought across Chinese territory by Russia and Japan
ch01.note: The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05), fought largely in Manchuria — Chinese soil — over rival claims to Manchuria and Korea; Japan’s victory was sealed by the Treaty of Portsmouth without China’s consent.
The 1905 revolution against the Russian tsar, touched off partly by defeat by Japan; its example encouraged constitutional agitation in China and pushed the Qing court toward concessions.

ch01.anchor: resembling the zemstvos under the czar in Russia
ch01.note: The zemstvos were elected local assemblies in tsarist Russia with real but tightly limited powers; Isaacs likens the Qing’s 1910 provincial assemblies to them for his mostly Western readers.

Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925), the Canton-born, Hawaii- and Hong Kong-educated revolutionary regarded as the founder of the Chinese Republic. His Revolutionary Alliance (Tungmenghui) led the anti-Manchu movement; he was briefly first provisional president in 1912 and later rebuilt the Kuomintang, whose fate is the subject of this book.

ch01.anchor: the Miao tribes in the southwest and the Muslims in the northwest
ch01.note: The Miao (Hmong) are a non-Han hill people of south and southwest China; the “Muslims” are the Hui and other Muslim communities of the northwest. Both mounted major revolts in the mid-nineteenth century amid the general upheaval.

ch01.anchor: especially in Hunan, Hupeh, and Szechwan
ch01.note: Three central and western provinces — modern Hunan, Hubei, and Sichuan — where the campaign to keep the railways in Chinese hands was strongest, and where the 1911 revolt would break out.

The Xinhai Revolution of 1911, which toppled the Qing and founded the Republic on January 1, 1912. Isaacs’s theme is that it was a “tiny push” that changed the label but not the social order, leaving power to provincial militarists (a real revolution; the dismissive reading is his own).

ch01.anchor: power passed into the hands of provincial or regional satraps
ch01.note: The warlords: after Yuan Shih-kai’s death in 1916 China fragmented among regional militarists with their own armies and taxes, often backed by rival foreign powers — the “warlord era” (c. 1916–1928) that is the backdrop to the revolution Isaacs will describe.

ch01.anchor: compelled to give way to Yuan Shih-kai
ch01.note: Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the Qing army’s strongest general, who secured the emperor’s abdication and then supplanted Sun as president in 1912, ruling as a dictator and briefly proclaiming himself emperor (1915–16). His maneuvering is Isaacs’s prime example of the 1911 revolution’s betrayal.

The Kuomintang (Guomindang, Nationalist Party), formed in 1912 out of Sun Yat-sen’s Revolutionary Alliance. It is the central actor in this book: allied with the Communists and Moscow from 1923, it turned on them in 1927 — the “tragedy” of Isaacs’s title.

ch01.anchor: a direct result of the Great War
ch01.note: The First World War (1914–18). With the industrial powers absorbed in Europe, foreign competition in Chinese markets eased and native industry surged, as Isaacs details in the figures that follow.

ch01.anchor: A telegraph line was laid between Shanghai and Tientsin
ch01.note: Tientsin (modern Tianjin), the great treaty port and gateway to Peking on the northern coast.

ch01.anchor: the revolt of the garrison at Wuchang
ch01.note: The Wuchang Uprising of October 10, 1911 — a mutiny of the New Army garrison at Wuchang, on the Yangtze — touched off the Xinhai Revolution; the date is still marked as the Republic’s “Double Tenth.”
Kiangsu (modern Jiangsu), the wealthy lower-Yangtze province around Shanghai and Nanking, long a center of silk production.

Hankow (part of modern Wuhan, with Hanyang and Wuchang), the great commercial city where the Han river meets the Yangtze; the projected Canton–Hankow trunk line would tie south China to the Yangtze. Hankow later becomes the seat of the left-Kuomintang government at the center of this book.

ch00a.note: In the text the name appears as Kuomintang, the customary spelling under the now outdated Wade-Giles system of transliteration.

The line comes from John Adams’s summation as defense counsel at the 1770 trial of the British soldiers charged in the Boston Massacre; Adams (1735–1826) later became the second president of the United States.

Harold R. Isaacs (1910–1986), the author of this book and the subject of the foreword. An American journalist, he lived in China from 1930 to 1935, wrote The Tragedy of the Chinese Revolution (1938) as his first book, and later taught politics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Leon Trotsky (1879–1940), with Lenin a leader of the Russian Revolution of October 1917 and the organizer of the Red Army; expelled from the Soviet Union by Stalin in 1929, he led the international opposition to Stalin until his assassination in Mexico in 1940. “Trotskyist” names that opposition. Trotsky wrote the introduction that follows.

Vladimir Lenin (1870–1924) led the Bolsheviks’ seizure of power in 1917 and headed the first Soviet government until his death. The “Leninist principle” that Isaacs came to reject is the one named in the next clause—that a single revolutionary party must hold sole power.

Joseph Stalin (1878–1953) succeeded Lenin as leader of the Soviet Union and ruled it as a dictator until his death. In Isaacs’s account the Comintern policy that led the Chinese revolution to catastrophe was Stalin’s; he is a central figure in Trotsky’s introduction and in the book.

In Trotsky’s theory a “workers’ state” is a country where capitalist property has been overthrown; he held that Stalin’s USSR remained one but had been “degenerated” or “deformed” by a ruling bureaucracy. Arnold Isaacs notes that his father came to reject even this qualified defense of the Soviet system.

ch00a.anchor: as the Bolsheviks conceived and constructed it
ch00a.note: The Bolsheviks were the wing of Russian Social Democracy led by Lenin; their 1917 revolution made them the ruling Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Trotsky’s introduction turns on the contrast between original “Bolshevism” and the bureaucratic rule that grew out of it.

Chiang Kai-shek (1887–1975) succeeded Sun Yat-sen as head of the Kuomintang and its army. He led the Northern Expedition of 1926–28, the campaign that reunified China from the south, then in April 1927 turned on his Communist allies—the “tragedy” of the title—and ruled Nationalist China until his defeat by the Communists in 1949 and retreat to Taiwan. He is the book’s central figure.

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), founded in 1921. On Comintern instructions it joined the Kuomintang in a “united front” from 1923; Chiang’s 1927 purge nearly destroyed it. It would win national power in 1949 and has ruled China since.

ch00a.anchor: the Communist movement’s international arm, the Comintern
ch00a.note: The Communist International, or Comintern (1919–1943), was the Moscow-directed federation of the world’s Communist parties. It ordered the Chinese Communists into—and held them in—their alliance with the Kuomintang, the policy this book sets out to expose.

Mao Zedong (1893–1976) led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in 1949 and ruled the People’s Republic until his death—a minor figure in the events of this book, but the ruler whose later campaigns, named just below, fell on the very intellectuals Isaacs had known. (Isaacs’s 1938 text uses the older spelling “Mao Tse-tung.”)

ch00a.anchor: the anti-Rightist campaign of the late 1950s
ch00a.note: A 1957 purge in which several hundred thousand Chinese—many of them intellectuals who had just been urged to criticize the Party—were branded “Rightists” and sent to labor, prison, or internal exile.

The upheaval Mao launched in 1966 and sustained until his death in 1976: a decade of mass persecution, factional violence, and the wrecking of institutions, aimed at his rivals and at supposed class enemies, with victims in the millions.

Jiang Qing (1914–1991), Mao’s wife and a leader of the Cultural Revolution. With three allies—the “Gang of Four”—she was arrested weeks after Mao’s death in 1976 and later convicted; the arrests marked the end of the Cultural Revolution.

ch00a.anchor: Deng Xiaoping was beginning to set China
ch00a.note: Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997) emerged after Mao’s death as China’s paramount leader and launched the market reforms and opening to the West that remade the country; 1980, the year of Isaacs’s return, was near their start.

A pointed reference to U.S. President Richard Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972, which opened relations between Washington and the People’s Republic while Isaacs, an old friend of the revolution, was still barred from the country.

ch00b.note: Historical materialism is the Marxist method that explains history through the development of the economy and the resulting struggle of social classes, rather than through ideas or great men. It is the framework underlying both Isaacs’s book and this introduction.

ch00b.anchor: Isaacs’ book represents a scientific work
ch00b.note: The introduction is itself a partisan document. Trotsky led the losing side of the very quarrel the book recounts—the opposition to Stalin and the Comintern—so his praise of Isaacs and his framework are those of an interested party.

ch00b.anchor: the present war between Japan and China
ch00b.note: The Second Sino-Japanese War, which Japan launched in July 1937 and which was raging as Trotsky wrote in 1938; it merged into the Second World War and ended with Japan’s defeat in 1945.

Trotsky’s name for the revolutionary upheaval of 1925–27—the subject of this book—counting the 1911 fall of the monarchy as the first. It runs from the May Thirtieth movement of 1925 (the strike wave set off when British-officered police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai) through the Northern Expedition (the 1926–27 military drive north from Canton) to the collapse of the Communist–Kuomintang alliance in 1927.

The dialectic is the mode of reasoning, taken by Marxists from Hegel, that sees things as developing through their own internal contradictions rather than as fixed. Trotsky contrasts it with the “common sense” empiricism he attributes to Anglo-Saxon thought.

ch00b.anchor: The English Revolution of the seventeenth century
ch00b.note: The English Revolution, or Civil War, of the 1640s, which overthrew and executed Charles I; Trotsky’s “Puritan revolution,” whose leaders justified themselves in the language of the Bible. He pairs it with the French Revolution of 1789 as the classic “bourgeois” revolutions.

In Marxist theory a “bourgeois” revolution is one whose historical task is to clear away feudal survivals and establish capitalist, democratic conditions—the work the English and French revolutions did. Trotsky’s whole argument is that in a backward country like China this task can no longer be carried out under bourgeois leadership.

“Semi-colonial” is the Marxist term for a country like China that keeps formal independence but is dominated economically—and partly politically—by foreign imperial powers. The distinction from an outright colony (India) is central to Trotsky’s classification of the backward countries.

The “national” bourgeoisie is the native capitalist class of a colonial country, as opposed to foreign capital. Trotsky argues it is too dependent on foreign finance to lead a genuine national revolution—the theoretical heart of his quarrel with the Comintern’s China policy.

ch00b.anchor: The petty bourgeoisie of the colonies
ch00b.note: The petty (small) bourgeoisie—artisans, shopkeepers, small traders—stands between the capitalists and the workers. Trotsky holds that in the colonies it is crushed by foreign competition and cannot play an independent political role.

The proletariat is the modern industrial working class, which owns no property and lives by wage labor. Marxists hold it to be the only class able to lead the revolution to the end and to establish its own class rule (the “dictatorship of the proletariat”); the claim that this holds even in backward China is the crux of the introduction.

In pre-revolutionary France the population was divided into three “estates”: the clergy, the nobility, and the Third Estate—everyone else, from peasants to the wealthy middle class. Its assertion against the first two opened the French Revolution of 1789.

The revolution of 1905 (a failed rising that won a limited constitution); the February Revolution of 1917, which overthrew the tsar; and the October Revolution of 1917, in which the Bolsheviks seized power. Trotsky treats their lessons as decisive for the twentieth century.

ch00b.anchor: the founder of the Russian Social Democracy, Plekhanov
ch00b.note: Georgy Plekhanov (1856–1918), the “father of Russian Marxism.” “Social Democracy” here means the Marxist workers’ movement before 1917, whose Russian party split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks; Plekhanov sided with the Mensheviks. Trotsky uses his two-stage theory of revolution as a foil.

The Narodniks (from the Russian for “the people”) were the nineteenth-century Russian agrarian socialists who looked to the peasant village commune as a road to socialism that would bypass capitalism; Plekhanov’s Marxists argued against them that Russia must first pass through capitalism.

ch00b.anchor: the legend later manufactured by the epigones
ch00b.note: “Epigones”—literally the lesser successors of a great generation—is Trotsky’s scornful term for Stalin and the other Bolshevik leaders who, he charges, distorted Lenin’s ideas after his death.

Lenin’s “April Theses,” issued on his return to Russia in April 1917, broke with the idea that the revolution must stop at a bourgeois-democratic stage and called for all power to the soviets—the workers’ and soldiers’ councils. Trotsky marks this as the moment Lenin’s view converged with his own.

Trotsky’s central theory: in a backward country the proletariat, not the weak bourgeoisie, must lead the democratic revolution, and having taken power it cannot stop at bourgeois limits but passes “uninterruptedly” into a socialist revolution bound up with the world revolution. Its supposed vindication and betrayal in China is the thread running through the whole introduction.

The Comintern’s formula for the Chinese revolution: an alliance of workers, peasants, urban petty bourgeoisie, and “national” bourgeoisie, used to justify keeping the Communists inside the Kuomintang. It is the specific doctrine Trotsky blames for the catastrophe of 1927.

Nikolai Bukharin (1888–1938), a leading Bolshevik theorist and, from 1926, head of the Comintern; with Stalin he directed the China policy Trotsky attacks. He was later a defendant in the Moscow show trials and was executed in 1938, the year this introduction was written.

ch00b.anchor: the argument of the Russian Mensheviks
ch00b.note: The Mensheviks held that backward Russia must first pass through a bourgeois-democratic stage, in alliance with the liberal bourgeoisie. Trotsky’s charge is that the Comintern made the Chinese Communists play the same role toward the Kuomintang.

ch00b.anchor: The party of the Social Revolutionaries
ch00b.note: The Socialist Revolutionaries (SRs), the largest Russian socialist party of peasant orientation, rivals of the Marxist Social Democrats; after 1917 they joined the moderate coalition the Bolsheviks overthrew.

ch00b.anchor: not yet then called the People’s Front
ch00b.note: The Popular (or People’s) Front was the Comintern’s policy, adopted in 1935, of broad alliances with liberal and socialist parties against fascism. Trotsky condemned it as a revival of the class collaboration that had wrecked the Chinese revolution.

“Revolutionary defeatism” was Lenin’s position in the First World War: that socialists should work for the defeat of their own imperialist government rather than support it. Trotsky credits it with keeping the Bolsheviks free of the wartime patriotism that swept up the other socialist parties.

Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925), founder of the Kuomintang, whose “Three Principles of the People” (nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood) were the party’s official doctrine. Trotsky calls them “reactionary scholastic” because the Chinese Communists were made to accept them as the price of joining the Kuomintang.
Actuel is French for “current” or “of present relevance”; Trotsky means that the history of 1925–27 bears directly on the war being fought as he writes.
“Mikado” is an old Western term for the Emperor of Japan; Trotsky uses it for imperial Japan, which he argues has arrived too late to build a lasting empire in Asia.

Professor Chen defined these categories as follows: “When a peasant family is barely capable of self-support from the land, and in its agricultural labour not directly exploited by, nor exploiting, others, we may say that such a family belongs to the class of middle peasants. The status of the middle peasants helps us to determine that of the other two classes of peasantry. When a peasant family hires one or more agricultural labourers by the day or by the season during busy times, to an extent exceeding in its total consumption of labour power that required by the average middle peasant family for self-support, or when the land which it cultivates surpasses in area the average of the land used by the middle peasant, we shall then classify this family as that of a rich peasant. Where we see families cultivating twice as much land as the middle peasants in their village, we safely classify them as those of rich peasants without further considering the labour relations. The poor peasants are comparatively easy to recognize. All peasant families whose number of cultivated mow (one mow is one-sixth of an English acre) falls below that of the middle peasants and whose members, besides living on the fruits of their own cultivation have to rely upon a wage income or some income of an auxiliary nature, belong to the poor peasants in general. Those poor peasants who do not cultivate any land, either their own or leased, but hire themselves out, or who cultivate a mere patch of land but have to support themselves chiefly by selling their labour power in agriculture, are called hired agricultural labourers, but still belong to the peasantry.” —Agrarian Problems in Southernmost China, Shanghai, 1936, p. 8.

ch02.anchor: the Bismarcks and the Louis Napoleons
ch02.note: Otto von Bismarck (1815–1898), who unified Germany from above, and Louis Napoleon (Napoleon III, 1808–1873), who seized power in France by coup in 1851: Isaacs’s shorthand for the authoritarian strongmen to whom a bourgeoisie frightened of revolution surrendered power after 1848.

The revolutionary municipal government that ruled Paris for some ten weeks in the spring of 1871 before being crushed with thousands of deaths. Marx analyzed it as the first working-class seizure of power, and Lenin took it as the model of the “dictatorship of the proletariat.”

ch02.anchor: the Second World Congress of the Communist International in 1920
ch02.note: The Comintern’s Second Congress (Moscow, July–August 1920) adopted Lenin’s “Theses on the National and Colonial Question,” quoted here, together with the supplementary theses of the Indian Communist M. N. Roy. It set the line — support for anti-colonial movements, but strict organizational independence within them — whose abandonment in China this book indicts.

ch02.anchor: The Social Democrats of the Second International
ch02.note: The Second International (1889–1916) was the pre-war federation of socialist and labor parties. Isaacs’s charge is that its major parties, when war broke out in 1914, backed their own governments rather than international workers’ solidarity — the collapse that prompted the founding of the Comintern, the Third International.

“War Communism” (1918–1921) was the Bolshevik regime’s emergency economy during the civil war: grain forcibly requisitioned from the peasants, industry nationalized, private trade suppressed. Its exhaustion of the country forced the retreat to the New Economic Policy.

ch02.anchor: the New Economic Policy to win a breathing space
ch02.note: The New Economic Policy (NEP), adopted in 1921, replaced forced requisitioning with a tax in kind and allowed limited private trade and small enterprise to revive an economy wrecked by war. It lasted until Stalin’s forced collectivization at the end of the 1920s.

ch02.anchor: the theory of “Socialism in one country”
ch02.note: The doctrine, advanced by Stalin from 1924 and elaborated by Bukharin, that a socialist society could be built in the Soviet Union alone without waiting for revolution abroad. It broke with the Bolsheviks’ original premise — and with Trotsky’s “permanent revolution” — that the Russian revolution could survive only as part of an international one; Isaacs makes it the root of the Comintern’s subordination of foreign revolutions to Soviet state interests.

Kulaks, the better-off peasants who hired labor or rented out land. Courted under the NEP, they were “liquidated as a class” in Stalin’s forced collectivization of 1929–33, with millions dispossessed, deported, or starved.
The Nepmen were the private traders and small entrepreneurs who flourished under the New Economic Policy; like the kulaks they were squeezed out when the NEP was ended.

ch02.anchor: the bourgeois Provisional Government in March 1917
ch02.note: The Provisional Government held power in Russia between the fall of the tsar in February/March 1917 and the Bolshevik seizure of power in October. Whether socialists should support it — the dispute recounted here — was the pivot of Lenin’s April Theses.

Alexander Martynov (1865–1935) and Moissaye Rafes (1883–1942), former Mensheviks who joined the Bolsheviks in the early 1920s and became Comintern commentators on China. Isaacs casts them as importing into Comintern policy the old Menshevik premise that the bourgeoisie must lead the bourgeois revolution.

ch02.anchor: the rotting autocracy of the Romanoffs
ch02.note: The Romanov dynasty ruled Russia from 1613 until the tsar’s abdication in 1917; “the Romanoffs” stands here for the imperial autocracy itself.

ch03.anchor: The shining phrases of Woodrow Wilson
ch03.note: Woodrow Wilson (1856–1924), U.S. president 1913–21, whose wartime rhetoric of national self-determination raised hopes across the colonial world. At the Paris Peace Conference he acquiesced in handing Germany’s Shantung holdings to Japan rather than returning them to China.

The May Fourth movement began with student demonstrations in Peking on May 4, 1919, against the Versailles decision to grant Japan the former German rights in Shantung. It broadened into a nationwide anti-imperialist and cultural awakening — strikes, boycotts, and a turn among intellectuals toward Marxism — that this chapter takes as the opening of the “second Chinese revolution.”

Syndicalism, a current of revolutionary trade-unionism holding that workers should overthrow capitalism and run society through their own unions, chiefly by the general strike, rather than through political parties.

Chen Chiung-ming (Chen Jiongming, 1878–1933), the Cantonese general who gave Sun Yat-sen a base in Canton and then, in June 1922, turned on him and drove him out. A federalist opposed to Sun’s centralizing nationalism, he was finally expelled from Kwangtung in 1925.

Li Ta-chao (Li Dazhao, 1889–1927), head librarian at Peking University and, with Chen Tu-hsiu, co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. Seized in a raid on the Soviet embassy in Peking, he was hanged by the warlord Chang Tso-lin in April 1927.
Chang Kuo-tao (Zhang Guotao, 1897–1979), a founding Communist and delegate to the 1921 congress, later a military rival of Mao. He broke with the party and defected to the Kuomintang in 1938.

ch03.anchor: laid before Sun Yat-sen by Dalin
ch03.note: Sergei Dalin (1902–1985), a young Soviet envoy sent in 1922 by the Young Communist International, the Comintern’s youth organization. His mission put the first proposal for a Communist–Kuomintang alliance directly to Sun, who refused a two-party bloc.

ch03.anchor: Maring, the first delegate of the Comintern in China
ch03.note: “Maring” was the alias of Hendricus Sneevliet (1883–1942), a Dutch Communist who had organized the left in the Dutch East Indies. As the Comintern’s first agent in China he devised the “bloc within” — Communists joining the Kuomintang as individuals — the policy this book indicts. He was later shot by the Nazis in occupied Holland.

Sarekat Islam (“Islamic Union”), a mass Indonesian organization founded in 1912 against Dutch colonial rule. Maring had helped build Communist influence in its left wing — the model he now proposed to apply in China.

ch03.anchor: the military strength of the warlord Wu Pei-fu
ch03.note: Wu Pei-fu (Wu Peifu, 1874–1939), the dominant militarist of North China in the early 1920s, backed by British interests. His troops carried out the February 7, 1923, massacre of the Peking–Hankow railway strikers described below.
The Anfu clique was the pro-Japanese faction around the militarist Tuan Chi-jui that controlled the Peking government in 1918–20, named for the Anfu Club through which it was organized.

ch03.anchor: sent by the Chita government and the Irkutsk Bureau of the Comintern
ch03.note: The Chita government (the Far Eastern Republic, a buffer state the Soviets maintained in Siberia, 1920–22) and the Comintern’s Irkutsk Bureau were Moscow’s early channels to East Asia. The “Irkutsk line” first backed the warlord Wu Pei-fu, before the Comintern turned to Sun Yat-sen.

Adolf Joffe (1883–1927), a senior Soviet diplomat. The joint statement he issued with Sun in Shanghai on January 26, 1923 — the Sun–Joffe Manifesto — sealed the Soviet–Kuomintang entente, Moscow conceding that China was not ready for Communism while pledging support for national unification.

Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the chief Soviet adviser to the Kuomintang from 1923. He reorganized the party on Bolshevik lines and steered its alliance with the Communists; when the alliance collapsed in 1927 he was recalled to Moscow, and he died in one of Stalin’s labor camps in 1951.

Founded near Canton in May 1924 with Soviet funds and advisers to build a loyal Nationalist officer corps. Its first commandant was Chiang Kai-shek, and it became the power base from which he came to dominate the army and the party.

ch03.anchor: thoroughly reorganized at its first national congress in January 1924
ch03.note: This was the Kuomintang’s First National Congress. Its admission of Communists as individual members inaugurated the “united front” — the alliance of the Nationalists, the Communists, and Moscow whose course this book traces.

Wang Ching-wei (Wang Jingwei, 1883–1944), a leader of the Kuomintang left and Chiang’s rival for Sun’s mantle. He headed the Wuhan government in 1927 and, from 1940, the Japanese-sponsored puppet regime at Nanking until his death.

The Washington Conference (November 1921–February 1922) produced naval-limitation and Pacific treaties among the powers, with a Nine-Power Treaty affirming China’s territorial integrity in principle. Chinese nationalists saw it as merely regularizing joint foreign domination — Wang Ching-wei’s “co-operative slow encroachment.”

Liao Chung-kai (Liao Zhongkai, 1877–1925), the most left-wing of Sun’s close aides and a champion of the Soviet alliance and the worker–peasant movement. He was assassinated by Kuomintang rightists in August 1925.

ch03.anchor: the massacre of February 7, 1923, at Chengchow, Honan
ch03.note: The “February 7” massacre: when railwaymen on the Peking–Hankow line moved to found a general union, the warlord Wu Pei-fu had the strike crushed by force, with dozens killed. It became a landmark in the labor movement’s calendar of martyrs. (Isaacs’s figure of sixty dead runs higher than most later estimates, which put it in the thirties.)

ch03.anchor: cradled in Haifeng, in the East River districts of Kwantung, by Peng Pai
ch03.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), who built China’s first mass peasant associations at Haifeng from 1922 and in 1927 led a short-lived Haifeng “soviet” — a peasant-run local government on the Russian model.

ch03.anchor: Britain’s Labour prime minister, Ramsay Macdonald
ch03.note: Ramsay MacDonald (1866–1937) headed Britain’s first Labour government (January–November 1924). His silence, for Isaacs, shows that a Labour ministry pursued the same imperial policy in China as its Conservative predecessors.

ch03.anchor: G. Voitinsky, Comintern delegate in China
ch03.note: Grigori Voitinsky (1893–1953), the Comintern envoy who had helped the Chinese Communists organize in 1920–21 and now, Isaacs argues, worked to subordinate the labor movement to Kuomintang leadership.

ch03.anchor: It was the afternoon of May 30.
ch03.note: The May Thirtieth incident: on May 30, 1925, British-officered police in Shanghai’s International Settlement fired on a crowd protesting the killing of a Chinese mill worker, killing twelve. The outrage set off a nationwide wave of strikes and boycotts — the May Thirtieth movement — that carried the revolution into its mass phase.

ch03.anchor: When they passed the Shakee Road Bridge
ch03.note: The Shakee (Shaji) massacre of June 23, 1925: British and French troops on Shameen, the foreign concession island at Canton, fired across the canal on an anti-imperialist march, killing fifty-two. It triggered the long Canton–Hong Kong strike and boycott described next.

ch03.anchor: A boycott of British goods and a general strike were immediately declared.
ch03.note: The Canton–Hong Kong strike and boycott ran about sixteen months, from June 1925 to October 1926 — among the longest strikes anywhere to that time. It paralyzed British Hong Kong and became the mass base on which the Kuomintang consolidated its power in the south.

ch03.anchor: the Yunnanese generals, Yang Hsi-min and Liu Chen-han

ch04.anchor: the members of the foreign Municipal Council
ch04.note: The Shanghai Municipal Council governed the International Settlement, the foreign-run district of Shanghai. Its councillors and voting ratepayers were overwhelmingly British, American, and Japanese; no Chinese sat on it until the three seats conceded, as related here, in 1926.

Stirling Fessenden (1875–1943), an American lawyer, chaired the Shanghai Municipal Council. In April 1927 he would open the way for Chiang’s purge by letting the Green Gang’s armed bands move through the International Settlement to fall on the Shanghai workers.

ch04.anchor: rose Yu Ya-ching, banker and compradore
ch04.note: Yu Ya-ching (Yu Qiaqing, 1867–1945), a leading Shanghai comprador, banker, and shipping magnate, was among the most powerful Chinese businessmen in the International Settlement and a financial backer of Chiang Kai-shek.

ch04.anchor: the staff of General Chen Chi-mei
ch04.note: Chen Chi-mei (Chen Qimei, 1878–1916), a close ally of Sun Yat-sen, was military governor of Shanghai after the 1911 revolution and Chiang Kai-shek’s early patron and sworn brother. He drew Chiang into both the revolutionary movement and the city’s underworld, and was assassinated in 1916 by agents of Yuan Shih-kai.

ch04.anchor: and Chang Ching-chiang, who was adding
ch04.note: Chang Ching-chiang (Zhang Jingjiang, 1877–1950), a wealthy financier and early bankroller of Sun Yat-sen’s revolution, became Chiang Kai-shek’s patron and political mentor and briefly chaired the Kuomintang’s Central Executive Committee. Nearly blind, he was reckoned one of the party’s “four elders.”

ch04.anchor: and gang in Shanghai, the Green Circle
ch04.note: The Green Gang (Qing Bang; Isaacs’s “Green Circle”) was Shanghai’s dominant secret society, controlling the opium traffic, gambling, prostitution, and much of the labor market. Chiang’s ties to it and to its bosses—Huang Chin-jung, the “Hwang Ching-yung” named here, and Tu Yueh-sheng—made it the instrument of the April 1927 slaughter of the Shanghai Communists.

Hu Han-min (Hu Hanmin, 1879–1936), a senior Kuomintang leader and a rival of Chiang’s for Sun’s mantle. Implicated in the August 1925 assassination of the left-wing leader Liao Chung-kai, he was eased out of Canton and sent to Moscow, as this chapter recounts; he returned to lead the party right and later headed the Nationalist Legislative Yuan before breaking with Chiang in 1931.

The Krestintern (Krestyansky Internatsional), the Communist International’s peasant organization, founded in Moscow in 1923 to draw the world’s peasantry behind Soviet policy; in practice largely a propaganda body.

ch04.anchor: The Sixth Plenum of the Executive Committee
ch04.note: The Executive Committee of the Communist International (E.C.C.I.) was the Comintern’s governing body between world congresses. Its Sixth Enlarged Plenum, meeting in Moscow in February–March 1926, adopted the resolution on China quoted here, which hailed the Canton government and bound the Chinese Communists more tightly to the Kuomintang.

Alexander Kerensky (1881–1970) headed Russia’s Provisional Government between the February and October revolutions of 1917—the moderate swept aside by the Bolsheviks. Calling the Kuomintang chiefs “Chinese Kerenskys” casts them as a doomed liberal interlude before a proletarian seizure of power that, in China, never came.

ch04.anchor: the Fengtien military, who had assumed control
ch04.note: Fengtien (Fengtian) is the old name for the Mukden region of Manchuria; the “Fengtien military” were the forces of the Manchurian warlord Chang Tso-lin, whose clique held Shanghai in 1925.

ch06.note: The Seventh Enlarged Plenum of the E.C.C.I., the Communist International’s governing Executive Committee, met in Moscow from November 22 to December 16, 1926, with China as its principal business. Its theses on the Chinese question, quoted throughout this chapter, were the Comintern’s fullest statement of the policy that governed the Chinese Communists on the eve of the 1927 rupture.

ch06.anchor: Tang Ping-shan, delegate of the Chinese Communist Party
ch06.note: Tang Ping-shan (Tan Pingshan, 1886–1956), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and its senior figure inside the Kuomintang. He sat on the Kuomintang’s Central Executive Committee and in 1927 became minister of agriculture in the Wuhan government; expelled from the Communist Party after the defeat, he helped found a “Third Party” and was reconciled with the Communists only late in life.

ch06.anchor: When P. Mif, later chief of the Stalinist experts
ch06.note: Pavel Mif (1901–1939), the Soviet Union’s rising China specialist and rector of the Sun Yat-sen University for Chinese students in Moscow. ch06.note: The Wanhsien Incident of September 5, 1926: British gunboats bombarded Wanhsien (Wanxian), an upper-Yangtze port, after a general allied to Wu Pei-fu seized two British steamers and their crews. The Opposition was not a homogeneous body. It was composed of a bloc of the original Left Opposition led by Trotsky and the so-called Leningrad Opposition of Zinoviev and Kamenev, who had originally united with Stalin in a “triumvirate” directed against Trotsky and had passed into opposition only in 1926. On the Chinese question important differences existed between the two groups and between Trotsky and Radek. As chairman of the Communist International Zinoviev had stood sponsor, as late as March 1926, for the resolution of the Sixth Plenum of the ECCI which canonized the bloc of classes in China. Stalin, in 1924–25, had produced the idea of “worker-peasant parties” for the East, and had identified the Kuomintang as the model example of such parties. Following him, Radek had regarded the Canton regime as a worker-peasant government. In the subsequent Opposition bloc, these differences intruded themselves. The Zinoviev group demanded the insertion of the formula of the “democratic dictatorship of the proletariat and peasantry” into the Opposition platform. The Trotsky group, over Trotsky’s protest, voted to accept it for the sake of the general agreement on other issues. Trotsky, whose single vote had been consistently cast in the Russian Politbureau against subordination of the Communist Party to the Kuomintang ever since 1923, continued, nevertheless, to present the essential kernel of his own views. The Stalin-Bukharin majority was able to contrast these views, with some effect, to those of Zinoviev, especially on the estimate of the attitude toward the Wuhan government and the question of withdrawal from the Kuomintang. In their speeches and articles on the Chinese question, both Stalin and Bukharin devoted much time and space to baiting the Opposition on the basis of its internal differences. While the real differences were by no means unimportant, the fundamental logic of the Opposition standpoint as a whole led directly to the demand for withdrawal of the Chinese Communist Party from the Kuomintang, and this was always recognized by its opponents as the essential Opposition demand. On the key question of the creation of soviets there was no difference in the Opposition ranks. References in the text to the Russian Opposition mean primarily the consistent Left Opposition led by Trotsky. Zinoviev, Kamenev, and Radek capitulated to Stalin in 1928, but this act, and others that followed, did not save them from the fate that awaited them at the hands of the Thermidorian reaction eight years later. The differences within the Opposition deserve further study which lies beyond the scope of this book. Those relating to the Chinese question are touched on briefly in a letter from Trotsky to Max Shachtman in 1930, published by the latter in his introduction to Trotsky’s Problems of the Chinese Revolution, pp. 18-20. Zinoviev’s views will be found in his “Theses on the Chinese Revolution,” printed the appendices to the same volume.

A comparison of this passage with several from Trotsky’s May 7 Theses is not uninstructive: “The political leadership, instead of embracing the masses of the army through soldiers’ soviets, has contented itself with a purely external copy of our political departments and commissars which, without an independent party and without soldiers’ soviets, have been transformed into an empty camouflage for bourgeois militarism.” Again: “One would at least think that the military coup d’état of Chiang Kai-shek had finally hammered into the minds of every revolutionist that trade unions separated from the army are one thing, and united workers’ and soldiers’ soviets…are quite another thing.” Again: “If we do not want to permit the bourgeoisie to drive a wedge between the revolutionary masses and the army, then soldiers’ soviets must be fitted into the revolutionary chain (of workers’, peasants’ soviets).”—Trotsky, Problems, pp. 49, 58, 78. The difference between Trotsky and Chiu Chiu-pei is that the former wrote these words in May 1927, when corrective action was still possible. Chiu Chiu-pei’s “confession” comes more than a year after the event. This is the difference between Marxism and empiricism.
